title: Alert Acknowledge Streaks per Responder
prompt: You are working with an observability platform tracking alert acknowledge time and MTTR. The schema has two tables: `responders` (id, name, on_call_days—a TEXT[] column listing weekdays they are scheduled, and created_date) and `alert_acks` (responder_id, ack_date, response_time_minutes—stored as TEXT). The `alert_acks` table may contain duplicate rows for the same (responder_id, ack_date) because a responder can acknowledge multiple alerts in the same day. Write a query that returns the id and name of every responder who has at least 5 consecutive days of alert activity, along with a cleaned display name, their first scheduled weekday, the month they were created (as a number), their average response time (rounded to 2 decimals), and a priority flag. The output columns are: responder_id, responder_name (trimmed and title-cased), first_on_call_day (the first element of the on_call_days array), created_month (the numeric month from created_date), avg_response_minutes (the average of response_time_minutes cast to numeric then rounded to 2 decimals), and priority_flag ('high' if avg_response_minutes is NULL or >= 60, otherwise 'normal'). A consecutive day streak means the responder acknowledged at least one alert on N days in a row with no gaps; duplicate same-day acknowledgments should be de-duplicated before counting consecutive days. Order the output by responder_id ascending.

display.context: You are working with an observability platform tracking alert acknowledge time and MTTR modeled on incident response workflows.
display.task: Write a query that returns the id and name of every responder who has at least 5 consecutive days of alert activity, along with a cleaned display name, their first scheduled weekday, the month they were created, their average response time, and a priority flag, ordered by responder_id ascending.

table_notes.responders: one row per on-call engineer with their id, name, scheduled weekdays, and creation date
table_notes.alert_acks: one row per alert acknowledgment with the responder id, acknowledgment date, and response time in minutes stored as text; may contain duplicate (responder_id, ack_date) rows because a responder can acknowledge multiple alerts in the same day

output_field_notes.responder_name: the responder's display name, trimmed of surrounding spaces and with each word capitalized
output_field_notes.first_on_call_day: the first weekday from the responder's scheduled on-call days array
output_field_notes.created_month: the numeric month (1-12) the responder was created
output_field_notes.avg_response_minutes: the average response time in minutes across all the responder's acknowledgments, rounded to 2 decimal places
output_field_notes.priority_flag: high if the average response time is NULL or 60 or more, otherwise normal

field_logic:
responder_name: built from name.
- trim surrounding spaces
- capitalize each word

first_on_call_day: built from on_call_days.
- take the first element of the array

created_month: built from created_date.
- extract the numeric month (1-12)

avg_response_minutes: built from response_time_minutes.
- cast each response_time_minutes text value to numeric
- compute the average
- round to 2 decimal places

priority_flag: built from avg_response_minutes.
- 'high' when avg_response_minutes is NULL or >= 60
- otherwise 'normal'
display.filter_note:
A responder is returned only when ALL of these are true:
- the responder has at least one streak of 5 or more consecutive days where they acknowledged at least one alert each day
- duplicate (responder_id, ack_date) rows in alert_acks are de-duplicated before detecting consecutive days

schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE responders (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), on_call_days TEXT[], created_date DATE); CREATE TABLE alert_acks (responder_id INT, ack_date DATE, response_time_minutes TEXT);
example_input_data: INSERT INTO responders (id, name, on_call_days, created_date) VALUES (1, '  alice cooper  ', ARRAY['Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday'], '2024-03-15'), (2, 'bob jones', ARRAY['Thursday', 'Friday'], '2024-04-20'), (3, 'carol white', ARRAY['Saturday', 'Sunday'], '2024-05-10'); INSERT INTO alert_acks (responder_id, ack_date, response_time_minutes) VALUES (1, '2024-06-01', '45'), (1, '2024-06-02', '50'), (1, '2024-06-03', '55'), (1, '2024-06-04', '60'), (1, '2024-06-05', '65'), (2, '2024-06-10', '30'), (2, '2024-06-11', '35');

composite_moves: dedupe same-day events with SELECT DISTINCT
apply row-number trick partitioned by entity: date - rn grp
group by entity and grp, HAVING COUNT >= N to find qualifying streaks
join dim table to streak entities using EXISTS or IN membership semantics
clean output columns with INITCAP, TRIM, array subscript, EXTRACT, cast, ROUND, COALESCE, CASE

hints: Start by de-duplicating the (responder_id, ack_date) pairs in alert_acks since one responder can acknowledge multiple alerts in the same day.
Use the row-number trick to group consecutive dates: subtract ROW_NUMBER() (partitioned by responder_id, ordered by ack_date) from ack_date to create a constant group identifier for each streak.

Group by responder_id and the streak group, filter with HAVING to keep only groups of 5 or more days, then join back to the responders table to pull the name and other attributes; use the array subscript operator for the first on-call day, EXTRACT for the month, and cast response_time_minutes to numeric before averaging.
answer_key: WITH base AS (SELECT DISTINCT responder_id, ack_date FROM alert_acks), date_groups AS (SELECT responder_id, ack_date, ack_date - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY responder_id ORDER BY ack_date)::int AS grp FROM base), streaks AS (SELECT responder_id FROM date_groups GROUP BY responder_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 5), responder_stats AS (SELECT a.responder_id, ROUND(AVG(a.response_time_minutes::numeric), 2) AS avg_response_minutes FROM alert_acks a GROUP BY a.responder_id) SELECT r.id AS responder_id, INITCAP(TRIM(r.name)) AS responder_name, r.on_call_days[1] AS first_on_call_day, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM r.created_date)::int AS created_month, rs.avg_response_minutes, CASE WHEN COALESCE(rs.avg_response_minutes, 60) >= 60 THEN 'high' ELSE 'normal' END AS priority_flag FROM responders r JOIN responder_stats rs ON rs.responder_id = r.id WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM streaks s WHERE s.responder_id = r.id) ORDER BY r.id;

_meta.scenario: an observability platform tracking alert acknowledge time and MTTR
